content: I'm not sure if general upper bounds on the expression lcm(1,..,n) specifically are in the project, but if you have log lcm(1,...,n) = Chebyshev psi (n), then we do have the estimate psi(n) < 1.11 n in the Blueprint. The proof is not formalized yet, however.

If we show

theorem foo (n : ℕ) : ArithmeticFunction.log (L n) = psi n := sorry

then using docs#ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt_le_log we could get an upper bound of log (n!) or n log n, which is a start

We have very nearly formalized the bound ψ x ≤ 6 * a * x / 5 + (log (x/5) / log 6) * (5 * log x - 5) for 30 ≤ x, where a = (7/15) * Real.log 2 + (3/10) * Real.log 3 + (1/6) * Real.log 5 is about 0.9213. See https://alexkontorovich.github.io/PrimeNumberTheoremAnd/blueprint/secondary-chapter.html#chebyshev-estimates-sec ; only a few minor sorries remain to finish this off. Ignoring the lower order term, this is a bound roughly of the form 1.105x1.105 x1.105x. The optimal constant (if one wants a bound that holds for all x>0x>0x>0) is ψ(x)≤1.03883x\psi(x) \leq 1.03883 xψ(x)≤1.03883x (due to Rosser and Schoenfeld), which is stated in the blueprint but for which no proof has yet been attempted. The slightly weaker ψ(x)≤1.11x\psi(x) \leq 1.11 xψ(x)≤1.11x, essentially due to Chebyshev, should be doable soon, the main remaining issue is how to deal with the medium range 30≤x≤10630 \leq x \leq 10^630≤x≤106.

docs#Chebyshev.psi_le already has the weaker bound psi x ≤ Real.log 4 * x + 2 * √x * Real.log x which is the same as bounding the lcm by 4n+2n4^{n+2\sqrt{n}}4n+2n​ as you initially noted.

It seems that Real.log (L n) = Chebyshev.psi n is not yet in Mathlib; I'll add it to Lcm.lean as some bonus results.

EDIT: docs#primorial_le_4_pow is closely related to the upper bound Ln≤4n+2nL_n \leq 4^{n+2\sqrt{n}}Ln​≤4n+2n​ since the primorial of nnn is actually most of LnL_nLn​ already (there is a correction term coming from the primes p≤np \leq \sqrt{n}p≤n​); this may be another route for your specific application.

I managed to find a low-tech proof of LCM (1..n)≤4n(1..n) \le 4^n(1..n)≤4n . (It can be viewed as a modern reformulation of an argument of Erdos in 1934.) If I can add it as part of my existing project (SSS) I will. Would (the formalization of) such a statement (or low tech proof) be of use to this project, even though it is not the strongest available?

So I will work on this, but the result is pretty slick, so I will share it here.

For another project I want bounds on some products of primes, namely for integer k, set kh=⌈k/2⌉kh = \lceil k/2 \rceilkh=⌈k/2⌉, then set R(k)={p:pR(k) = \{ p : p R(k)={p:p prime and kh<p≤k}kh < p \le k \}kh<p≤k}. I then use the bound ∏p∈R(k)p∣(kkh)≤4k−kh\prod_{p \in R(k)} p \mid {k \choose kh} \le 4^{k-kh}∏p∈R(k)​p∣(khk​)≤4k−kh, and I iterate this by setting j=⌈k/2r⌉j = \lceil k/2^r \rceilj=⌈k/2r⌉ and then ∏j<p≤kp=∏0≤i<r[∏p∈R(⌈k/2i⌉)p] \prod_{j<p \le k} p = \prod_{0\le i<r}[ \prod_{p \in R(\lceil k/2^i \rceil)} p ]∏j<p≤k​p=∏0≤i<r​[∏p∈R(⌈k/2i⌉)​p] divides ∏0≤i<r(⌈k/2i⌉⌈k/2i+1⌉)≤∏0≤i<r4⌈k/2i⌉−⌈k/2i+1⌉=4k−j \prod_{0\le i<r} {{\lceil k/2^i \rceil} \choose {\lceil k/2^{i+1} \rceil}} \le \prod_{0\le i<r} 4^{{\lceil k/2^i \rceil} - {\lceil k/2^{i+1} \rceil} } = 4^{k - j} ∏0≤i<r​(⌈k/2i+1⌉⌈k/2i⌉​)≤∏0≤i<r​4⌈k/2i⌉−⌈k/2i+1⌉=4k−j. This is straightforward and should not be too hard to formalize.

Now try the same thing with S(k)={p:pS(k) = \{ p : p S(k)={p:p prime and there is e>0e>0e>0 so that kh<pe≤k}kh < p^e \le k \}kh<pe≤k}. It turns out ∏p∈S(k)p=lcm(1..k)/lcm(1..kh)∣(kkh)\prod_{p \in S(k)} p = lcm(1..k)/lcm(1..kh) \mid {k \choose kh}∏p∈S(k)​p=lcm(1..k)/lcm(1..kh)∣(khk​), and now one can iterate this enough times to derive not only lcm(1..k)≤4k lcm(1..k) \le 4^k lcm(1..k)≤4k but also lcm(1..k)≤4k−c(log2(k))2lcm(1..k) \le 4^{k - c(log_2(k))^2}lcm(1..k)≤4k−c(log2​(k))2 for an explicit value of ccc, after paying attention to the difference between the various (kkh){k \choose kh}(khk​) and 4k−kh4^{k-kh}4k−kh.

At the rate I am going, I will have a version to submit in a few months (still learning Lean). If someone else wants to formalize this, be sure to reference Erdos 1934 (On a Theorem of Sylvester and Schur), plus the reformulation above. The idea isn't original, but the reformulation (to the best of my knowledge) is original.
